items.summary: Jensen Huang, Nvidia's co-founder and chief executive, was reinstated to his role after a period of being effectively ousted. His removal stemmed from two events: a New York Times report on October 29 alleging he had been targeted by a Chinese spy plot involving Alice Huang, an executive linked to Singapore-based Megaspeed International, which the newspaper said may have funneled information to Beijing and steered Nvidia AI chips there; and his November 9 admission of an extramarital affair with Ms. Huang, prompting a board probe. China's Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun rejected the spying allegations as baseless. On November 12, amid falling shares, the board met on leadership matters and Huang resigned as CEO, with CFO Colette Kress serving as interim; his share price continued to decline while US Congress members concerned about national security implications summoned him for testimony. On Monday, Nvidia announced its board had unanimously agreed—with input from senior US government officials—to reinstate Huang, sending shares soaring. In a statement, Huang said he was honoured to return and lead the company at the start of what he called a new industrial revolution. The reinstatement followed a petition signed by major US tech billionaires and public comments urging Nvidia to restore him; Trump posted that he had spoken directly to the board and called the decision correct and proper, adding the government had no reason to believe Huang engaged in unlawful conduct or posed a national security risk while wanting Nvidia to continue reviewing its export control compliance. Critics expressed concern about Trump's intervention: Democratic senator Chuck Schumer said Democrats would investigate any wrongdoing by the administration, Huang, other executives, and anyone selling out national security for financial gain; Professor Charles Elson of the Weinberg Centre for Corporate Governance told the ABC that reinstating Huang signals no accountability for his actions and could create an environment where some people are above the law or set a meaningless code exposing the organisation to legal risk; and Consumer Federation of America AI and privacy director Ben Winters called the president's intervention highly inappropriate and another sign of lax regulation. Huang is still expected to face scrutiny, including testimony before a US Senate banking committee next month.
items.title: Nvidia Board Reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO After Spy Allegations

items.summary:
A global coalition of more than 155 child safety organizations and experts called on Amazon and eBay on Monday (November 23, 2026) to immediately stop selling toys equipped with artificial intelligence chatbots over concerns about risks to children's safety and development. In an open letter addressed to Amazon CEO Andy Jassy and eBay CEO Jamie Iannone, the coalition urged the retailers to suspend sales of AI-powered toys marketed to children under 16 until independent testing establishes their safety. The coalition also called on both companies to warn customers who have already purchased such toys and offer refunds.

The letter noted that more than 50 AI toys were recently found on Amazon's US marketplace, while 28 were identified on its UK platform in late October. Some products were marketed to children as young as three despite connecting to general-purpose chatbots intended for older users, while others advertised features such as voice cloning and tracking children's emotional development.

The coalition cited tests in which AI toys gave inappropriate sexual responses and instructions involving matches and knives, while also raising concerns about privacy violations. It warned that children could develop unhealthy emotional attachments to AI companions, with the long-term effects on their development and mental health remaining unknown.

"These products should be shown to be safe before they reach children, not withdrawn one at a time after harm is found," the coalition said. Fairplay's Young Children Thrive Offline Program Director Rachel Franz added that retailers have been pulling AI toys from shelves individually when called out, but "it's not enough." The coalition asked both companies to respond by Christmas so the information could be shared with lawmakers and parents.

The appeal comes as California prepares to introduce a four-year ban on the manufacture and sale of AI companion toys intended for children under 16, beginning January 1, 2027.
items.title: Over 150 Child Safety Groups Urge Amazon, eBay to Halt AI Toy Sales

items.summary: South Korea and China have largely completed talks to expand their free trade agreement, with new commitments covering entertainment, tourism, and financial services. The announcement came last week during talks between South Korean President Lee Jae Myung and Chinese President Xi Jinping at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen. Technical details, translations, and legal reviews still need to be completed before the expanded agreement can be formally signed, China's commerce ministry said.
items.title: South Korea and China Agree Wider Trade Deal Covering Entertainment

items.summary: Treasurer Jim Chalmers announced that the government will deliver a modest net savings in its upcoming mid-financial year economic and fiscal outlook (Myefo) update, though he described it as not being a “slash and burn” budget. The Myefo is expected to be released between early December and the handing down of the Bondi royal commission, with Chalmers noting that substantial but carefully targeted savings will avoid impacting payments or sensitive parts of the economy. Shadow treasurer Tim Wilson cast doubt on this promise, asserting that past government savings claims have resulted in saving $2 while spending $3, and proposed an alternative plan to save more than $31bn by cutting climate and housing programs.
items.title: Labor Promises Modest Net Savings in Mid-Year Budget Update Amid Rental Affordability Decline

items.summary: The House ethics committee released a 19-page report on Monday concluding that California Democrat Jimmy Gomez engaged in sexual misconduct, finding 'substantial evidence' he made unwelcome sexual advances and had sexual contact with a House staffer. The panel determined Gomez made unwanted sexual advances toward the staffer twice—once involving physical contact and once where he was described as being 'forceful' with her in his congressional office—and stated that his conduct reflected a broader environment of misconduct and toxic working conditions on Capitol Hill. The report issued no specific recommendations, instead noting that the House should take whatever action it deems appropriate to police its members' behavior. Gomez, who represents parts of Los Angeles and was set to leave Congress in January after losing his re-election bid earlier this month to Democratic socialist Angela Gonzales-Torres, announced he would resign on December 1. He said he had 'strong disagreements with the committee's report and its conclusions,' but took full responsibility for the 'personal mistakes I committed outside of my marriage' and noted that he cooperated with the investigation voluntarily. The allegations against Gomez are described as part of a series of ethics investigations this year in which representatives resigned or lost their bids, including Eric Swalwell (California), who stepped down after sexual assault and misconduct allegations ended his gubernatorial campaign; Tony Gonzales (Texas), who resigned after admitting an affair with an aide who later died by suicide; Chuck Edwards (North Carolina), who announced he would not seek re-election after a report found he fostered a hostile work environment through gifts and attention to two young female staffers; Cory Mills (Florida), defeated in the Republican primary amid ethical lapses, against whom a Florida judge granted a protective order at his former girlfriend's request in October 2025; and Max Miller (Ohio), who lost his re-election bid amid an ethics investigation into drug use and domestic abuse allegations tied to his divorce from Emily Moreno. The report was published after Gomez had already announced his resignation, which he dated December 1.
items.title: House Ethics Panel Finds Evidence of Jimmy Gomez's Sexual Misconduct; He Will Resign

items.summary: In the occupied West Bank, Palestinian ambulance drivers navigate Israeli checkpoints and road closures while transporting patients to hospitals. According to rights groups, these obstacles have caused wait times for hospital access to spike, and medics working on these routes report having been attacked.
items.title: Palestinian Ambulance Drivers Report Israeli Checkpoints as Dangerous Obstacles in West Bank

items.summary: CGTN's First Voice commentary reports that protests are spreading across European nations, with France at the center of escalating unrest. In Paris, streets have become gripped by tear gas and fireworks while gigantic paintings inside museums glorify the Enlightenment era once associated with equality, fraternity, and solidarity. The column poses open questions about what these young people, working-class citizens, and even politicians are protesting against—whether it is inflation, deteriorating living conditions, or a loss of hope for the younger generation's future. According to CGTN, this unrest has spread beyond France to other European countries including Spain and Germany, with 'rage' described as the best word to characterize the continent's current mood.
items.title: Protests Erupt Across Europe Amid Escalating Unrest

items.summary:
A coordinated night-time attack by Ukraine's SBU intelligence agency and armed forces struck Russia's corvette Merkury in a Mediterranean harbour near Benghazi, Libya — anchored roughly 2,000 miles from Moscow. The ship and an accompanying cargo vessel were hit while berthed in eastern Libya, territory controlled by pro-Moscow warlord Khalifa Haftar. Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky described the operation as 'an exemplary operation,' while Russia called it 'a dangerous escalation.'

The attack follows a suspected Ukrainian drone strike on a Russian dry-cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland, which the Kremlin labeled an act of terrorism, and earlier long-range drone strikes on Russia's Baltic oil terminal at Ust-Luga. Ukraine has also targeted deep inside Siberia — including last year's Operation Spider's Web, involving a lorry that released explosive drones near a Russian strategic nuclear bomber airbase — and has struck Russian mercenaries from the Africa Corps in Africa.

The United Nations mission in Libya expressed 'deep concern,' noting that Libya is not a party to the Russia-Ukraine war. The International Maritime Organisation (IMO) has condemned attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz throughout this year, prompting questions about whether the Benghazi strike sets a dangerous precedent for future operations.

The wider conflict has already spread across Europe as the fifth anniversary of Russia's full-scale invasion approaches. On Friday, Russian projectiles landed inside Poland — just 60 miles from an Anglo-French exercise planned following an eventual ceasefire — which Prime Minister Donald Tusk called 'a deliberate provocation.' This is not the first time Russian munitions have entered Polish territory.

Romania and Moldova have been repeatedly struck by overflying Russian drones targeting Ukraine's Black Sea ports, while Bulgaria and Romania suffered maritime drone attacks on commercial shipping just offshore. In Romania, a NATO member, fast jets scrambled to intercept incoming drones amid suspicion that the incursions are not accidental. The three Baltic states — Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania — border Russia and have faced anonymous attacks on military industrial facilities blamed on agents acting for Moscow; Russia in turn suspects Estonia of complicity in Ukrainian drone overflights.

The article frames these developments as part of a rising trend in hybrid warfare involving largely unattributable operations such as cyber attacks, warehouse fires, and the dispatching of surveillance and explosive drones. This autumn, Germany's Leipzig-Halle airport — used by Ukraine's cargo aircraft for resupply — was targeted by three explosive drones discovered before anyone was hurt, alongside other incidents involving explosive packages sent across Europe targeting Germany, Poland and the UK. Moscow denies involvement in these attacks.
items.title: Ukraine's Benghazi Strike on Russian Ship Signals Wider Spread of the War

items.summary: In a CGTN episode titled 'Empty Suitcases In, Full Stories Out,' host Liu Xin joined American author Zak Dychtwald to visit Shenzhen—the APEC host city—to explore how China's accessible innovation is gaining global appeal. The discussion highlighted the 'China Haul' trend and what has been described as a tech-tourism boom, noting that products such as electric vehicles, cameras, and hair dryers are becoming increasingly common in daily life overseas and serving as an introduction to a multidimensional China.
items.title: CGTN Host and Author Explore Made-in-China Innovation in Shenzhen

items.summary: Speaking with FRANCE 24's Sharon Gaffney, Oleksandra Matviichuk—Director of the Centre for Civil Liberties and Nobel Peace Prize laureate—described today's war in Ukraine as 'a war of unmanned machines, AI, total transparency of the battlefield, mass drone attacks and long range weapons.' She stated that this character of conflict means humanity must rethink how to protect human beings.
items.title: Nobel Laureate Matviichuk: Ukraine War Is a Battle of Unmanned Machines and AI

items.summary: Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned on Sunday that Americans should expect more technology outages and disruptions as companies and government agencies replace aging systems. Speaking on CNN's 'State of the Union,' Clayton said, "And as part of that ongoing upgrade, we are going to have glitches, gaps, interruptions in service... That is going to happen." The comments came days after President Donald Trump attributed a recent spate of technology failures to upgrades of companies' technology systems. Clayton noted that these upgrades were necessary to improve performance and cybersecurity as technological advances strain older systems. A string of technology failures this month disrupted critical US systems, including a nationwide halt to air travel, a Microsoft outage affecting email services, a technical glitch impacting several major banks, and a temporary disruption to the National Security Agency's network. On ABC's 'This Week,' Clayton reiterated that these outages were not the result of coordinated or state-sponsored actions, attributing them instead to technical upgrades. He declined to discuss specifics of separate reports of cyberattacks on the FBI and Department of Agriculture, saying he expects investigators to provide answers "in due course."
items.title: US Intelligence Chief Clayton Warns of More Tech Outages During System Upgrades

items.summary: A fire at Makofi Hotel near the northern tip of Zanzibar spread to adjacent buildings, injuring several hotel staff but leaving all 183 tourists unharmed. Thick black smoke from thatched roofs whipped across white sands as strong winds carried flames into nearby resorts, restaurants and shops on Nungwi Beach. Eyewitness mobile footage captured buildings roaring with fire while tourists and locals scrambled down the beach—some hauling suitcases, others helping to fight the blaze—until firefighters drawn from three stations subdued it after about three hours.
items.title: Fire Engulfs Beachfront Hotels on Zanzibar's Nungwi Beach

items.summary:
This story was co-published with El Pais and Puente News Collaborative. The article follows two men—Carlos Joaquín, a Guatemalan asylum seeker from Guatemala living near Dallas, Texas, and Balin, a Nicaraguan biology student-turned floor sweeper and hairdresser in Milwaukee—who came to fear deportation after the Trump administration's mass-deportation program intensified over roughly the past year. The author frames their experience as "the sharpest persecution of a specific community of people on U.S. soil in decades." Although Joaquín and Balin held asylum permits, they believed they were on an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) list with no other immigration protection.

The Trump administration claims it has deported "millions" of "criminal" migrants since taking office; however, the Migration Policy Institute's independent estimate put combined ICE and CBP deportations at approximately 980,000 for the first 18 months through July 2026. The institute's study also showed that about 80 percent of deportees have no criminal record—a figure Joaquín and Balin cite to underscore their claim they are not criminals.

Joaquín crossed into the U.S. from Ciudad Juárez in El Paso with his then-10-year-old son Fernando, having sold all he owned—his land, chickens, and cattle—to a smuggler who helped them make the 2,000-mile trek north; they were later released by Border Patrol with a work permit while their case went through courts. Balin arrived in Milwaukee via Texas Gov. Greg Abbott's plan to transport more than 100,000 migrants from the border to Democratic-run cities such as New York, Los Angeles, Denver, and Chicago—a move costing at least $148 million in taxpayer dollars.

As ICE agents swarmed across both communities, Joaquín grew anxious: his commute became too dangerous, he skipped required check-ins because many people were detained when they showed up, and he began buying used cars, land, and cattle to prepare for possible departure. He planned to watch a round-of-16 World Cup match at AT&T Stadium in Arlington with his son before that event.

Balin described the summer as "the quiet period," staying home, going off social media, and arranging clandestine commutes while discussing contingency plans with his now-pregnant girlfriend. He avoided large stadiums like American Family Field where the Milwaukee Brewers play, cut hair at a nondescript barbershop earning money "entre tinieblas"—in the shadows—and considered leaving for dairy work in rural Wisconsin.

After the November 3 midterm election—a blue-wave result that pushed out key Republican politicians tied to Trump's deportation program—the author expected Joaquín would be emboldened but could not locate him. His boss, who refused to give his name, said he may have been deported or self-deported and confirmed "Carlos Joaquín" was not his real name; the man asked anyone who found him to tell him they miss him. The author spent weeks scraping social media until finding Joaquín's accounts frozen, messaged friends, family, and a church with no response by mid-November, and noted his WhatsApp last showed use on July 2—before he saw the Spain-Portugal World Cup match.

Balin remained reachable; after being told at an ICE meeting that he had 20 days to leave the country, he planned to go underground before reconnecting briefly with family in Managua if deported and then moving to Mexico City. He lamented that Trump's elevation of Stephen Miller—architect of the deportation plan—to chief of staff sealed his fate, concluding "We're still in the eye of the storm." The piece is written by Alfredo Corchado, executive editor and correspondent for Puente News Collaborative.
items.title: Trump's Great Persecution: Carlos Joaquín and Balin, life in the eye of the deportation storm

items.summary: China's second domestically built large cruise ship, Adora Flora City, embarked on its maiden commercial voyage on Sunday, departing from Guangzhou in Guangdong Province for a six-day, five-night journey to Hong Kong and Hue, Vietnam. Carrying more than 3,800 passengers aboard the vessel—which measures 341 meters in length with a gross tonnage of 141,900 tons, features 2,130 cabins, and can accommodate up to 5,232 passengers—the ship represents another step in China's efforts to expand cruise tourism and boost consumption. Construction began in August 2022; operated by Adora Cruises under China Tourism Group, the ship was delivered in Shanghai on November 6 and completed its first trial voyage on November 9. Shi Dai, chairperson of China Tourism Group, said the company is using cruise operations to develop integrated cultural tourism products and travel experiences aimed at setting a new benchmark for sea vacations.
items.title: China's Second Domestically Built Large Cruise Ship Begins Maiden Voyage

items.summary: Singer Parastoo Ahmadi and four members of her band and production team were each flogged with 74 lashes by Iranian authorities in the city of Qom, according to a member of their defence team who spoke to the BBC. The punishments followed Ahmadi's December 2024 concert at which she wore a sleeveless dress while livestreaming; Iran bans public performances by women and requires headscarves and modest clothing. In June this year, a criminal court in Qom convicted Ahmadi and eight others of 'offending public decency' through the publication of 'obscene and indecent material,' charges they denied. The defendants were sentenced to 74 lashes each plus two-year bans from audiovisual activities and leaving the country. An appeals court rejected their appeal at the end of September, confirming the sentence, according to her lawyers. On Monday, a defence lawyer told the BBC that Ahmadi and four male co-defendants—identified by another lawyer as Soheil Faghih-Nasiri, Amin Taheri, Amirali Pirnia and Mohsen Lashkari—had been flogged at the third branch of the Criminal Sentence Enforcement Office in Qom. The lawyer said his team attempted to overturn or reduce the sentence and postpone enforcement, but the enforcement branch insisted on carrying it out immediately. Bahar Ghandehari, director of advocacy at the US-based Center for Human Rights in Iran (CHRI), condemned Ahmadi's flogging as a violation of her fundamental rights and an attempt by Iranian authorities to suppress women's freedoms.
items.title: Iranian Authorities Flog Singer Parastoo Ahmadi for Performing Without Hijab

items.summary: On Monday, authorities in divided Libya's east called on the United Nations to investigate claims that Ukrainian military forces were present in western Libya. The request came alongside a complaint lodged over alleged Ukrainian attacks on two Russian ships off Benghazi. According to FRANCE 24 reporter Emerald Maxwell, the strikes occurred Sunday and are claimed by Kyiv, amid reports that Ukraine is increasing its strikes against Russia far from the front lines of the war.
items.title: Divided Libya's East Calls for UN Probe into Claims Ukrainian Forces Present in West

items.summary: The Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), under the Ministry of Home Affairs, issued an advisory warning that leaving a WhatsApp Web session logged in on a shared computer can expose users' accounts to unauthorised access. Issued by I4C's National Cybercrime Threat Analytics Unit, the guidance urged users—particularly those using office computers or other devices accessible to others—to log out manually after every session. The advisory explained that someone who gains access to an active session could read private messages, view contacts and group chats, and send messages while posing as the account holder, potentially enabling fraudsters to contact friends, relatives or colleagues from a trusted account. I4C noted that a WhatsApp Web session can remain active even after the browser tab or window is closed, advising users to avoid signing in from cyber cafes, public kiosks, hotel business centres or borrowed computers and instead use private windows on trusted devices while logging out before closing them. The advisory also cautioned against exchanging confidential information through WhatsApp Web, urged users to treat unexplained account activity—such as messages they did not send or unexpected replies—as a serious concern, and recommended keeping operating systems, browsers and security software updated while avoiding suspicious downloads and untrusted applications. Queries sent to Meta, which owns WhatsApp, remained unanswered.
items.title: India's I4C Warns Users to Log Out of WhatsApp Web on Shared Computers

items.summary:
Mexican security forces arrested Fausto Isidro Meza-Flores—known as 'El Chapo Isidro'—on Saturday after an exchange of heavy gunfire around his compound in Sinaloa state. He is accused of smuggling large amounts of fentanyl, methamphetamine, and cocaine into the US over more than two decades and was listed among the FBI's 10 most-wanted fugitives, making him eligible for extradition to the US.

President Claudia Sheinbaum held a press conference on Monday emphasizing that the operation was planned and led by Mexican forces without participation from US agents on the ground. 'The areas in which we coordinate with the US are security and intelligence,' she said, adding that 'they do not conduct operations in Mexico.' However, Sheinbaum confirmed that Mexican officials requested deployment of a drone to help with the operation.

Washington has not claimed responsibility for the strike; instead, officials celebrated joint coordination on the arrest. US Ambassador to Mexico Ronald Johnson pointed to intelligence sharing in a post on X. The Guasave Cartel headed by Meza-Flores trafficked drugs into the US since at least 2000 and more recently fought a turf war against a faction of the larger Sinaloa Cartel, according to the US Treasury Department.

The operation killed 16 alleged associates of Meza-Flores and detained another 16, Defense Minister Ricardo Trevilla said. More bodies were found after officials originally reported that seven suspected gang members were killed along with four soldiers. Another ten federal agents were injured in an operation that mobilized hundreds of troops, special forces, and several Black Hawk helicopters.

The US government had offered a $5 million reward for information leading to Meza-Flores' arrest or conviction. The arrest marks Mexico's highest-profile cartel operation since the February capture of Nemesio 'El Mencho' Oseguera, whose death from injuries during transport following a military raid was reported.

Over the past two years, Sheinbaum has faced intense pressure from US President Donald Trump to take more aggressive action against the country's powerful drug cartels. After meeting with Sheinbaum in China last week, Trump reiterated that the cartels are 'running Mexico,' an assertion the Mexican leader rejects.
items.title: Mexico Arrests Suspected Cartel Leader Using US Intelligence, No US Agents on Site

items.summary: Nvidia's board confirmed the return of CEO Jensen Huang, following President Donald Trump's public urging on November 22 and a confirmation that his reinstatement posed no national security risk. The market response was immediate: at Monday's open, Nvidia shares rose around 30% to 31%, reaching approximately $164.91 from Friday's close of $125.53.
items.title: Jensen Huang Returns to Nvidia: Winners and Losers

items.summary:
On November 23, US President Donald Trump posted an AI-generated meme on his Truth Social account at 11:32 am ET depicting NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang in the photograph taken moments after the July 2024 assassination attempt against Trump in Butler, Pennsylvania. The digitally altered image replaces Trump with Huang, showing him with a bloodied face surrounded by Secret Service agents; instead of Trump's raised fist, Huang is depicted holding a red bra, and the American flag has been replaced by a black NVIDIA logo. The post carries a watermark from satirical meme account @GRANDOLDMEMES and was shared without an accompanying caption.

The image appeared hours after NVIDIA's board reinstated Huang as president, CEO and director on November 12, reversing his departure 11 days earlier amid scrutiny of reported personal relationships and concerns over US export-control compliance. Trump had publicly supported the return, describing Huang as valuable to the company and US economy, and separately praised the board's decision while stating the government had no evidence Huang engaged in unlawful conduct.

The reinstatement has not ended scrutiny of NVIDIA's export-control compliance; Huang is expected to face congressional questioning while the company's internal review continues.
items.title: Trump Shares AI-Generated Meme Depicting Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang in Butler Photo

items.summary: The Union Home Ministry (MHA) issued an advisory cautioning users to avoid leaving WhatsApp Web logged in on public or shared computers, warning that cybercriminals could exploit the active session to hijack accounts and conduct fraud. The advisory was released by the National Cybercrime Threat Analytics Unit (NCTAU), part of the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C). It advised users not to simply close a browser window or tab but to manually log out after each session, avoid official work on WhatsApp Web, use incognito and private browsing modes when necessary, refrain from logging in via cyber cafes or borrowed computers, stay alert to unusual account activity, keep devices secure with updated software, and avoid suspicious downloads. The MHA advisory coincides with a warning note issued by the Border Roads Organisation (BRO), under the Ministry of Defence, regarding suspected cyber espionage by Pakistan-based intelligence operatives through WhatsApp groups targeting Indian defence personnel. According to the BRO, spies allegedly gained access using compromised Indian mobile numbers and joined security groups as silent members to eavesdrop on conversations. The BRO also flagged an incident in which a civilian staff member reportedly conversed with someone posing as a Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) scientist named 'Soniya' through a WhatsApp group titled 'All India Defence Civilian Mutual Transfer Posting,' allegedly sharing sensitive defence information for money. The BRO advisory was dated November 17, while the MHA advisory was published on November 23, 2026.
items.title: India's Home Ministry Warns of WhatsApp Web Security Risks Amid Suspected Cyber Espionage

items.summary: Reserve Bank of India Governor Sanjay Malhotra on Monday emphasized the importance of responsible and sustainable credit growth by non-banking finance companies (NBFCs), urging them to put customers first as they expand their business. These remarks came in the backdrop of NBFCs recording a 20.5 per cent year-on-year growth in credit during FY26, according to figures cited alongside his statements.
items.title: RBI Governor Flags Importance of Responsible, Sustainable NBFC Credit Growth

items.summary: On November 23, Nvidia announced that its board had unanimously voted to reinstate Jensen Huang as the company's president, CEO and board director with immediate effect. The board said it was satisfied with Huang's candour and leadership ability after a series of discussions and meetings with him, and stated—based on input from senior levels of the US government—that his reinstatement does not pose a national security risk. Board chair Harvey C. Jones said the company believes Huang is the right person to lead Nvidia and that his return serves the interests of stockholders, employees, partners and customers; he will continue as board chair while Colette Kress remains interim CEO and CFO. In response to the announcement on X (formerly Twitter), Elon Musk posted "The mistake has been corrected" shortly after Nvidia confirmed Huang's immediate return, followed by a second post stating "It is done," which did not name Huang or Nvidia. When praised for standing by Huang after his removal as CEO, Musk replied that those who support you when the chips are down are your real friends and called fair-weather friends worthless. Jensen Huang said he was honored to return and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a new industrial revolution, thanking board chair Harvey Jones, Colette Kress, executive staff, employees, shareholders, industry leaders, partners worldwide and his family. Nvidia also stated that its independent board committee would continue investigating reports that Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort, noting that Huang supports the investigation and is committed to cooperating with it.
items.title: Nvidia Reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO; Elon Musk Reacts

items.summary: On November 23, Nvidia's board unanimously voted to reinstate Jensen Huang as president, CEO, and director—just 11 days after he resigned on November 12 amid reports that his wife Alice Huang was a Chinese intelligence asset. The article notes the board cited Huang's candour and input from unnamed senior US government officials in its decision; it attributes the specific claims about the affair with an Nvidia executive to The New York Times (November 11) and the romantic relationship report to the Financial Times (November 7). Between resigning and returning, Nvidia's stock fell nearly 14% on November 20 to $125.53—its worst day since January 2025—with shares having lost about $2.7 trillion in market value from their October 6 peak; Moody's lowered its Aa1 outlook to stable on November 18, and a "Stand With Jensen" petition reached 178,000 signatures by November 16 with Elon Musk publicly backing Huang. On November 14, Altimeter Capital's Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management's Gavin Baker requested a slow CEO search while holding about $2.13 billion of Nvidia stock between them; the article attributes their measured stance to those firms rather than presenting it as fact. Shares jumped more than 25% in premarket trading on November 23, though they remained below the $166.19 close when Huang resigned. The New York Times reported on November 18 that Megaspeed bought more than $4 billion of Nvidia chips with Alibaba as a customer and backer; the article attributes this to both The New York Times (November 18) and The Information's report linking Nvidia to Alice Huang in 2022. On November 16, the US Justice Department and Commerce Department announced a criminal investigation into Megaspeed, while Bessent said several agencies had favored listing it for months; on November 17, Nvidia stated it was not shipping Hopper data centre products including H200 processors to China. The article reports that Huang faces closed-door interviews with US House committees on December 1 and Senate Banking Committee testimony requested by Tim Scott on December 3, and attributes the SEC investigation report to The Wall Street Journal (November 17) and California Attorney General Rob Bonta's subpoena to November 19.

items.summary: The Supreme Court of India granted bail to Irfan Siraj Pada, one of the convicts in the 2002 Godhra train burning case, citing his serious cardiovascular disease. A bench comprising Justices MM Sundresh and PB Varale suspended his sentence after accepting that his medical condition was factually correct; the state had also accepted it. Pada has been in jail for around 18 years.
